question: My node fires every quarter of an hour, but all morning its log shows each run giving up without doing anything. How do I see why, and is something broken?
answer:

The node's implementation cycle runs on a crontab line fired every 15 minutes by default (`schedule.cycle_interval_minutes`, default `15`) — that's your "quarter of an hour" cadence. A run that does nothing is a **stand-down**: `agent-cycle.sh` logs an event with `"event": "stand-down"` and a `reason` field to `~/.local/state/poetic-agents/log.jsonl` and exits cleanly, every time.

To see why, run:
```bash
jq -r 'select(.event == "stand-down") | "\(.ts)  \(.reason)"' \
  ~/.local/state/poetic-agents/log.jsonl | tail -5
```
(or `tail -f` the same file to watch it live).

Whether this is "broken" depends on the `reason` string you see. It's very likely *not* broken: the pipeline has a cost-saving "no-op short-circuit" — if nothing the Co-Ordinator reads (commits, issues, PRs, etc.) has changed since the last time it answered "nothing to do," the cycle stands down again without re-asking, for the price of a few `gh` calls rather than a full LLM pass. That's expected behaviour on a quiet morning, and it's self-correcting: `none_selected_recheck_hours` forces a real check periodically regardless, and any detectable change — even a repo the Script couldn't read cleanly — breaks the short-circuit immediately. A reason string in that "nothing changed" family (or a `disabled.json` switch, back-pressure, usage-limit cooldown, etc. — see the stand-down reason ladder) is normal; a reason suggesting a credential, auth, or read failure is the one worth investigating further.

2. **Let any in-flight cycle finish** — disable this node only with `agent-cycle.sh --disable 'decommissioning' --this-node --for 2h` and wait until `--status` shows idle. Use `--this-node` (not plain `--disable` or `--drain`) since there's no surviving node that needs to `--enable` it back.

question: I merged a fix to the pipeline's code a while ago, but one node still shows the old version on the dashboard. How does a new version reach the nodes, and when should I start worrying?

By default, **none** — `merge_autonomy` ships as `human` fleet-wide and stays there until you deliberately raise it; at that level the pipeline never approves or merges anything, and every PR waits for your click.

If you've opted a repository into a higher trust level, the picture changes:

- **`agent-merges-routine`** — the Script itself merges (no human click) any PR graded `low`/`medium` complexity (by default, via `merge_autonomy_routine_complexity`) that came from a source listed in `merge_autonomy_routine_sources` and touches no path in `merge_autonomy_routine_protected_paths`. Regardless of level, three cases always force a human click: a PR the merge queue ever dequeued for a reason other than merging, a PR whose latest round answered feedback through `landing-refusals`, and one whose source the landing stage can't read back. A `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review from your own account also blocks landing unconditionally at every level.

So: with a fresh/default install, nothing merges without you. If you've raised `merge_autonomy` to `agent-merges-routine` or `agent-merges-all` for a repo, then routine (and, at the top level, even protected-path) PRs can land via the Script's own merge, approved by the Approver App rather than a person — that's the case where a PR lands without a human sign-off. You can force everything back to `human` instantly with `agent-cycle.sh --kill-merge-autonomy "<reason>"`.

question: What am I going to be paying for in model usage? Which part is the expensive part, and does it still cost money when there is nothing to do?
answer:
This answers it fully.

Your model spend is spread across several stages, each running on a different tier of Claude model:

- **Co-Ordinator** — Haiku, runs every cycle (default every 15 minutes) just to check for work.
- **Implementer** — Sonnet/Haiku, does the actual coding.
- **Reviewer** — Sonnet normally, escalating to Opus if the Implementer graded the work `complexity:high`.
- **Approver** — Sonnet/Opus/`claude-fable-5` across its three tiers (`approver_model_default`/`_complex`/`_critical`).
- **Enabler** — Opus (`enabler_model`), described in the config table (README.md:516) as "the most expensive model here," though it's only engaged rarely, on long-blocked items.
- **Refiner** — Haiku, writes specs for unscoped items.

The **Enabler (Opus)** is explicitly flagged as the most expensive model, but it runs infrequently. The **Approver**'s `approver_model_critical` tier (`claude-fable-5`) is called "the rarest and most expensive tier," only hit when a PR has been refused twice in a row.

As for paying when there's nothing to do: yes, but it's deliberately kept cheap. Every cycle, even one that finds no work, calls the Co-Ordinator (Haiku) to say "nothing to do" — README.md explains this costs "about 2½ minutes of Haiku" per call. The `none_selected_recheck_hours` setting still forces a real Haiku call periodically regardless, so a quiet pipeline is never silently stuck — just cheap while it waits.

question: My branch only edits one of the prompt files, which is just Markdown. Will merging it build a new image and roll it out to the nodes, and how can I check before I push?
answer:
Yes — a `prompts/*.md` edit is treated as code, not documentation, so merging it will build and roll out a new image. `prompts/*.md` isn't in the inert allowlist in `scripts/is-docs-only.sh` (its `is_inert()` only whitelists things like `docs/*` excluding the `-SPEC.md` files, `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `TECH-DEBT.md`, `LICENCE`, and `deploy/docker/README.md`); anything else, prompts included, falls through to `*) return 1`, meaning "not docs-only." ```bash
git diff --no-renames --name-only main...HEAD | ./scripts/is-docs-only.sh

question: shellcheck is clean on my laptop, but the shell-lint check fails on my pull request. What is CI doing differently, and how do I reproduce it before pushing?
answer:
Two things are likely different from running `shellcheck` directly on your laptop:

1. **CI lints with `-x` (follow sources) on every file, unconditionally.** The `shell-lint` job sets `LINT_SHELL_FOLLOW_MIB: 0`, which disables `scripts/lint-shell.sh`'s memory-budget guard entirely, so every script is checked together with everything it `source`s via `# shellcheck source=` directives, parsed as one program. On your laptop, if memory is tight (no cgroup/container ceiling, low `MemAvailable`), the guard may instead lint some files *without* `-x` ("degraded") or skip them altogether — so findings in a sourced module, or in a variable that crosses a sourcing boundary, simply aren't surfaced locally.

2. **CI uses a pinned shellcheck version, `v0.10.0`**, not whatever version is installed on your laptop. A newer or older local `shellcheck` can disagree with CI on findings.

To reproduce CI's check exactly, run:

```bash
LINT_SHELL_FOLLOW_MIB=0 ./scripts/lint-shell.sh
```

making sure your local `shellcheck --version` matches `v0.10.0` (the pinned version CI installs, per `.github/workflows/shellcheck.yml`). The job also runs `./scripts/check-brace-default-trap.sh` as a separate step — worth running too, since it catches a shape (`${var:-word}`) that shellcheck itself doesn't.

Sources: scripts/lint-shell.sh (header comment, "THE SIZE GUARD" / "LINT_SHELL_FOLLOW_MIB set to exactly `0` disables the guard outright"); .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml ("Lint every shell script in the repository" step, `LINT_SHELL_FOLLOW_MIB: 0`, and the `SHELLCHECK_VERSION`/`SHELLCHECK_SHA256` env block).

I have enough to answer the question comprehensively.

The spec splits this across a few requirements in `docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md`:

- **Requirement 4a** ("Per-installation prompt overrides") governs what goes *into* a stage's assembled prompt: every stage's prompt is built by `lib/prompt-overrides.sh`'s `stage_prompt_text`, not a bare `cat prompts/<stage>.md`, so `config.json`'s `prompt_overrides.<s>.extend`/`.replace` (and, for Implementer/Reviewer, `repos[].prompt_overrides`) can add to or substitute the shipped file. Tested by `test/prompt-overrides.test.sh`.
- **Requirement 4b** covers the Co-Ordinator-specific `@@WORK_SOURCES_TABLE@@` marker, rendered from `config.json`'s `repos` array rather than hand-written.
- **Requirement 4c** ("An assembled prompt reaches its stage on stdin, never in argv") is the delivery mechanism: every `claude -p` invocation gets the prompt via a here-string on stdin, never as an argv string, because Linux's `MAX_ARG_STRLEN` (131072 bytes) would otherwise fail the `execve` once a prompt grows past it. Tested by `test/stage-prompt-delivery.test.sh`, which asserts delivery at a size the old argv approach couldn't carry and that both cycle scripts share the one `run_claude_stage` launcher.
- **Requirement 4d** ("One stage launcher, and it streams") specifies the actual launcher, `run_claude_stage` in `lib/stage-run.sh`, used by both pipelines, running `claude --output-format stream-json --verbose` in its own process group and producing the `<stage>.stream.jsonl`/`.out`/`.out.stderr` trio.
- **Requirement 45/45a/45b** mandate that every shipped stage prompt contain a byte-identical `## Untrusted external content` block (delimited by `<!-- untrusted-content:start/end -->` markers) warning the stage that forge-authored text is data, not instructions. This is pinned mechanically by `test/prompt-untrusted-framing.test.sh`, which lifts the block from the spec and from every named prompt and fails on any mismatch, missing marker, or duplicate.

Sources: `docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md`, requirements 4a–4d (prompt assembly and stdin delivery) and 45/45a/45b (`## Untrusted external content`); `test/prompt-overrides.test.sh`, `test/stage-prompt-delivery.test.sh`, and `test/prompt-untrusted-framing.test.sh`.

question: Which requirement governs the merge budget — what it counts and what happens at and past the cap — and which tests pin it?
answer:
This confirms `test/merge-budget.test.sh` as the dedicated pin for requirement 2.3c, with `test/landing-wiring.test.sh` and `test/backpressure-wiring.test.sh` likely covering its wiring into the landing/back-pressure flow.

## Answer

The merge budget is governed by **requirement 2.3c** in `docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md` ("The merge budget"), implemented in `lib/merge-budget.sh`.

- **What it counts:** `merge_budget_window_status` counts, per repository, the pull requests carrying `PR_LABEL` that were merged by the Approver App's login within a **rolling 24-hour window** of `mergedAt` (scoped via GitHub's own `merged:>=<cutoff>` search qualifier, not filtered after the fact). `merge_budget_per_day` sets the cap — fleet-wide default with a per-repo `repos[]` override — and `0` means unlimited, skipping the count entirely.
- **At the cap:** `merge_budget_decide` returns `hold` when `count == cap`. The PR still gets reviewed/approved normally, but landing does not arm — it queues in the visible backlog (the oldest open, non-draft, label-carrying PR is surfaced via `merge_budget_oldest_waiting`).
- **Past the cap:** if `count > cap` (an anomaly a correct governor should never see), the decision is `hold` with `anomaly: true`, which freezes the repository down to `agent-approves` (never all the way to `human`) via the fleet flag `fleet/merge-budget-freeze-<slug>.json`. The App still reviews; only automatic landing stops, and other repos are unaffected. `merge_autonomy_effective_level` reads this freeze and caps the configured autonomy level accordingly.
- An unreadable count instead returns `refuse`.

**Tests that pin it:** `test/merge-budget.test.sh` is the dedicated suite — it exercises all four `merge_budget_decide` outcomes (cap 0 arms with no `gh` call, under-cap arms, at-cap holds, over-cap holds-with-anomaly), the `already_armed` same-pass tally, and the freeze state machine (`merge_budget_freeze_state`/`_set`/`_clear`). Its wiring into the broader landing/back-pressure flow is additionally covered by `test/landing-wiring.test.sh` and `test/backpressure-wiring.test.sh`.

question: The Enabler's per-item claims are never released, which looks like a lock leak. Which design decision explains that, which requirements implement it, and which check proves the shortened retry?
answer:
I have what's needed to answer.

The "never released" claims are intentional, not a lock leak.

**Design decision:** requirement 35c's note explains that the per-item Enabler claim is a *tombstone*, not a lock. It's taken via `lib/claim.sh` under the pseudo-slug `enabler` (key `<repo>__<item>__<epoch of B>`), and it stops a failed engagement (timeout, garbage final message, omitted item) from being re-examined next cycle. Releasing it outright would let the very next cycle re-engage the same unchanged items at Opus prices for nothing, so the only way out is `lib/claim.sh gc` sweeping it once `claim_ttl_hours` elapses — bounding cost at "one failed attempt per TTL."

**Requirements that implement it:** requirement 35c (the never-released claim and its rationale) together with requirement 37, "Failure containment" — when the Enabler engagement fails even after requirement 9e's salvage attempt, the Script backdates that item's claim with `lib/claim.sh expire` instead of releasing it, which shortens the tombstone's floor from the full `claim_ttl_hours` down to about one cycle interval (the next `gc` sweep), while still never actually releasing the lock.

**Check that proves the shortened retry:** `test/claim.test.sh`, in the block headed `--- expire: a discarded engagement's tombstone is backdated, not released ---`. It asserts that `claim.sh expire` leaves the registry entry in place (not removed), backdates its `ts` to `1970-01-01T00:00:01Z` (far past `claim_ttl_hours`) while preserving the claimed item, and then confirms "gc retires an expired claim on its very next sweep."

question: My log is full of `stand-down` events whose reason begins `no-op short-circuit: no work source has changed since the Co-Ordinator found nothing to do at …`. Is the pipeline stuck, and how would I tell if it is actually missing work?
answer:
This is not stuck — that reason text is the normal output of the pipeline's cost-control optimization ("no-op short-circuit," requirement 3b of `docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md`). Before launching the Co-Ordinator each cycle, the pipeline fingerprints every input the Co-Ordinator's verdict could depend on (head SHA, issues/workflows/open-PR digests, tech-debt, claims, blocked/void, abandoned drafts, merge conflicts, etc.). If the most recent `none-selected` event already carries that same fingerprint and is younger than `none_selected_recheck_hours`, it logs a `stand-down` with that reason and skips launching the Co-Ordinator entirely — so seeing many of these in a row just means nothing in any tracked source has changed since the last time the Co-Ordinator genuinely looked and found nothing.

To tell whether it's actually missing work rather than correctly idling, you need to check two things:

1. **Is the fingerprint claim actually true?** The spec is explicit that this is a narrow, provable claim ("every input is byte-identical to when it last declined"), not a claim that there's no work — so the risk is a source left out of the fingerprint map, which would "silently stall" the pipeline with no error, just tidy stand-downs and no PRs. Check `lib/noop-skip.sh`'s `NOOP_CANON_JQ` and the source-to-signal map in requirement 3b to confirm the thing you believe changed (a new commit, a relabelled/reassigned issue, a workflow conclusion flip, a closed claiming PR, a stale draft crossing `abandoned_draft_after_hours`, a base going `CONFLICTING`, etc.) is one of the covered inputs.
2. **Force a real check.** Either wait past `none_selected_recheck_hours` (after which the short-circuit is bypassed and the Co-Ordinator is asked unconditionally, armed or not), or make a change to one of the fingerprinted inputs — if it's being tracked correctly, the very next cycle will bust the fingerprint and actually launch the Co-Ordinator rather than stand down.

Sources: `docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md`, requirement 3b ("No-op short-circuit (cost control)").

If instead the issue is about a re-flagged specification disagreement or a tactical decision (depending on your `escalation_autonomy` setting), the body will say so explicitly, and your answer is the same: resolve the underlying question and close the issue to trigger the next pass.

question: The log shows `claim-lost` events — mostly with `cause: "held"`, a few with `"pr-held"`, and one burst with `"unreachable"`. Do any of these mean something is broken, and what does the cycle do after one?
answer:
No, none of these three `cause` values indicate a broken pipeline — all three are expected, handled outcomes of claim contention, not errors.

- **`held`** — a peer node genuinely holds the item-keyed claim first. This is healthy contention: the work is already being done, just by someone else.
- **`pr-held`** — the same healthy contention, but on the *second*, PR-keyed claim a node takes right after winning a finishing-source item claim (so two nodes can't both work the same PR under different refs). It's named separately from `held` purely so a reader can tell which of the two claims a peer holds.
- **`unreachable`** — GitHub couldn't be reached at all for that claim attempt. This *is* the one that signals a problem (an outage), not contention — "no work is being done by anyone," as the spec puts it.

What the cycle does next: on any miss it fails closed and moves on to the next candidate. If every candidate in a cycle is lost, the cycle stands down — with reason "every candidate is already claimed elsewhere" if the misses were `held`/`pr-held`, or a distinct outage-flagged reason ("GitHub could not be reached for any candidate — this is an outage, not contention") if every miss was `unreachable`. The stand-down event's structured `cause` field reflects this too: a `raced` stand-down (from `held`/`pr-held` losses) chains into another selection cycle under the Finish-then-continue bound, whereas an `unreachable` stand-down does not chain — it would just hit the same outage again. A win that follows one or more `held` losses is also logged as a "recovered race" via a `race_losses` count on the `selection` event.

So: the `unreachable` burst is the one worth investigating (a GitHub/network outage during that window); the `held`/`pr-held` entries are just the fleet's claim mechanism working as designed.

question: The dashboard's void list shows one of my items as void, with a reason saying the work is already done on `main`, but I am sure it has regressed. What does void mean, and how do I get the pipeline to look at it again?
answer:
Found it — this is documented clearly in README.md.

"Void" means the pipeline has concluded there's no work left to do on that item: either it's already done, or its premise was false. By design, void is permanent and no agent can ever clear it on its own — the only evidence that would ever surface is "it's already done," which is exactly the reason it was voided, so letting an agent clear it would just cause the item to be rediscovered forever.

To get the pipeline to look at your item again (since you believe it's actually regressed), label any issue or pull request that names the item with `unvoided`, in that item's repo:

```bash
gh pr edit 92 -R Poetic-Poems/poetic --add-label unvoided
```

(substitute your own PR/issue number and repo). The next cycle reads the label, figures out which items that issue/PR names (from its branch, title, and body — or, for an issue, its own number), and reopens any of them that are void — putting the item back in the Co-Ordinator's pool in that same cycle. You can leave the label in place afterward; it's self-limiting and only reopens voids recorded before it was applied, so it can't be accidentally fired twice. If there's still no work when the pipeline looks again, the Implementer will simply void it again — this time with its own fresh evidence. Only a human can apply this label — no pipeline stage ever does.

Sources: README.md, section "Unsticking an item" (the "Void" bullet and the paragraphs beginning "To reopen a void item").

question: The pipeline has put `pw::needs-refinement`, `blocked` and `blocked:needs-refinement` on one of my issues. What is it telling me, and if I just take the labels off will it start work on the issue?
answer:
This tells you the pipeline looked at the issue and decided it doesn't name enough of a work order to act on — "Tidy up the sync script" with no end state, a question with no acceptance criteria, something waiting on a decision only you can make. It recorded the item as blocked for that reason and stamped all three labels (`needs-refinement`, `blocked`, `blocked:needs-refinement`) onto the issue so a filtered issue list shows you the same thing the pipeline's own log holds. It stays off the candidate list like any other blocked issue. After a few cycles' grace the Enabler looks at it and either writes a spec itself (clearing the labels), opens a separate escalation issue asking you something only you can decide, or leaves it alone if you've already deliberately parked the decision.

Taking the labels off yourself does **not** make it eligible again — only works the other way around: if *you* had applied `needs-refinement` to flag it yourself, removing that label does clear the block. But when the pipeline is the one that applied all three labels (as here), they're a one-way projection of the block already recorded in its own log, not a second way to change that state — removing them does nothing. To actually unblock it you need to either let the Enabler specify it, answer its escalation issue, or otherwise resolve the underlying "this needs more detail" problem yourself (e.g. editing the issue with goal/scope/acceptance criteria) so the pipeline's own recheck or next Co-Ordinator pass clears the block.
